newsitem.title: TURKMENISTAN: Turkmens to auction horses to revive famous breed.
newsitem.headline: Turkmens to auction horses to revive famous breed.

text.p: The former Soviet republic of Turkmenistan plans to start holding international auctions of its famous Akhal Teke racehorses and hopes that earnings from the sales will help revive the beautiful national breed.

"We will offer for sale Akhal Teke horses, and proceeds will enable us to keep and select other pure-breed horses," Annaguly Nurgeldyev, head of the state company Turkmen Horses, said in an interview with the Vecherny Ashgabat daily on Sunday.
He said the first auction of the breed -- famous for its stamina, speed and form -- would be held soon at the main national hippodrome in the Turkmen capital Ashgabat.
On Sunday the hippodrome hosted celebrations to mark the official national Holiday of the Turkmen Horse.
The colourful gala, introduced by presidential decree in 1995, showed the millenium-old cult of the noble horse is still alive in the desert Central Asian state.
Thousands of gleeful spectators crowded into the stalls in the morning to watch races of horses selected from Turkmenistan's leading breeding farms.
Race winners -- cheered by the crowd as national heroes -- were awarded national hand-made carpets and live rams.
But the celebration was soured by the fact that the future of the Akhal Teke horse is threatened by a lack of funds to support Turkmenistan's horse-breeding industry.
Turkmens blame seven decades of Soviet rule for the decay of their national pride.
In 1927, Turkmenistan had over 2,000 such horses but it now has only around one third of this number.

An economic programme "To catch up with and pass the West" introduced in the 1950s by then Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev had tragic consequences for Akhal Teke racers and sacrilegious overtones for the Turkmens.
The order, issued in Moscow in 1956, commanded the slaughter of horses to boost the Soviet Union's overall output of meat.

Instead of potential hard-currency earnings people were offered tonnes of horse sausage. The Communist party paid no attention to the fact that Turkmens are the only Central Asian people who traditionally do not eat horse meat.
In 1986 local Communist party apparatchiks issued a decree banning the slaughter of horses and even allowed breeding on private farms.
The overnight collapse of the Soviet Union in late 1991 made Turkmenistan an independent state, and an Akhal Teke horse is now at the centre of its national emblem.
But the horses are more than a revered symbol of national pride and history. They are also a subtle foreign policy tool.

The impoverished country with a population of around four million and huge reserves of natural gas wants to attract big Western investment but does not forget that it is in Asia and a part of the Moscow-dominated Commonwealth of Independent States.
So Turkmen horses have been given to Russian leader Boris Yeltsin, British Prime Minister John Major, the late French president Francois Mitterrand and Iranian President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani.
